:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The **gradient** of a multivariable function is analogous to the derivative of a single-variable function.

For a function $f(x,y)$ whose partial derivatives exist at a point $(x,y),$ the **gradient vector** is denoted $\nabla f(x,y)$ and can be found by computing the vector of partial derivatives:

 

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f (x,y) =  \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \mathbf i + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \mathbf j
                              
}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find $\nabla f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,\pi)$ given that $f(x,y) = (x - y)\cos y.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y-(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the gradient at the specified point, we substitute $(x,y)= (1,\pi)$ into the above, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(1,\pi ) & ={f}_{x}(1,\pi )\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(1,\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +(1-\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
For a function of three variables $f(x,y,z)$, the gradient of $f$ is given by the vector

$$\eqalign{ \nabla \! f (x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z)\ \mathbf i + f_y (x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z (x,y,z)\ \mathbf k. }$$

For a function $f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$ of $n$ variables, its gradient is usually given as a column vector:

$$\nabla f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = [\begin{aligned}{f}_{{x}_{1}} \\ {f}_{{x}_{2}} \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: The Gradient of a Function of More Than Two Variables

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla g(x,y,z)$   at $(2,-1,3)$ if $g(x,y,z) = x^2 + xyz.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =2x+yz \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =0+xz \\  & =xz \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =0+xy \\  & =xy\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+(xz)\text{ }j+(xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇g(2,-1,3) & =(2(2)+(-1)(3))\text{ }i+2(3)\text{ }j+2(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =1\text{ }i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)= (y-4)\ln (x-2),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\frac{y-4}{x-2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j = 0 \  \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{x-2}=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y-4=0,$ which means $y=4.$  From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x-2)=0,$ which means that $x=3.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf  0$ at the point $(3,4).$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Since the gradient of a function of several variables is made up of partial derivatives, we can expect it to have properties that are similar to partial derivatives.

Assume that $f$ and $g$ are functions whose first-order partial derivatives exist and are continuous on some open domain, and that $a,b,$ and $c$ are real constants. Then, the gradient has the following properties:

- Constant rule:  $\nabla c = \mathbf 0$

- Linearity: $\nabla (af + bg) = a \nabla\! f + b\nabla\! g$

- Product Rule: $\nabla(fg) = g \nabla\! f + f \nabla\! g$

- Quotient Rule: $\nabla \left( \dfrac{f}{g}\right) = \dfrac{ g \nabla\! f - f \nabla\! g}{g^2}$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y) g(x,y)$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\sqrt{xy},\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by

$$
\nabla [fg] = g \, \nabla\! f  + f \, \nabla\! g.
$$

Using the product rule shown above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+xy(\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j).\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient

For a multivariable function, the existence of the gradient implies continuity.

A sufficient condition for the gradient ![](images/3a/3a172b4fd0180b172579ebac50f73d8dfb75a219a02b610f666d1a4e446592a2.svg) to exist is that the partial derivatives ![](images/f2/f20807159d7e3d172a1ed9d92b8001a4c186e78ef3b8423592c75e44b633ec88.svg) and ![](images/f4/f423cce200533b35d0f6df2d4a6f5e917529276e749a7ab4995930d64559c98d.svg) both exist in a neighborhood of ![](images/52/527e0abeb684dd24d8c92e45425542080c4c9493b9460bb89753fef3226c1f92.svg) and are continuous at ![](images/52/527e0abeb684dd24d8c92e45425542080c4c9493b9460bb89753fef3226c1f92.svg).

Therefore, if ![](images/f2/f20807159d7e3d172a1ed9d92b8001a4c186e78ef3b8423592c75e44b633ec88.svg) and ![](images/f4/f423cce200533b35d0f6df2d4a6f5e917529276e749a7ab4995930d64559c98d.svg) both exist in a neighborhood of ![](images/52/527e0abeb684dd24d8c92e45425542080c4c9493b9460bb89753fef3226c1f92.svg) and are continuous at ![](images/52/527e0abeb684dd24d8c92e45425542080c4c9493b9460bb89753fef3226c1f92.svg), then ![](images/bc/bc562d54615dad55d095db2afed7626f62ff7ebf0ab6c5d45471b77ac30b6398.svg) is continuous at ![](images/85/853e57b0bf9a8f7c16e59d37575ae23ac4028ed66b30720af9d7d49ab595c91b.svg)

**Watch out!** The continuity of the partial derivatives is crucial. The existence of the partial derivatives alone does not imply that a function is continuous at a point.
